subtopic: Buoyancy, Archimedes' Principle and Relative Density
stem:
For performing an experiment to verify Archimedes' principle, a student used a spring balance with a zero error of 4 g wt. He used it to measure the weight of a solid metallic block as shown in the figure below. The solid metallic block was then lowered in water contained in an overflowing jar and the water displaced by this block was collected in a graduated or measuring cylinder as shown in the figure.

(The figure shows two setups: in (a) the metallic block hangs from a spring balance in air; in (b) the same block hangs from the spring balance while fully immersed in an overflow jar, and the water pushed out of the jar's spout is collected in a measuring cylinder beside it.)

Four students A, B, C and D while performing an experiment on establishing the relation between the loss of weight of a small solid when fully immersed in tap water, and the weight of water displaced by it, used four different shapes of overflow cans containing water as shown. The arrangement that would give correct results is that of student:

(The figure shows four overflow cans with side spouts: (A) a conical flask filled with water; (B) a cylindrical beaker filled to the spout level; (C) an inverted-cone shaped vessel; (D) a wide cylindrical beaker filled exactly up to the level of the spout opening.)

Three students A, B and C determined the volume of a solid by immersing it in water in overflow cans set up as shown. The result obtained will be wrong for:

In A and B the can sits on a raised stand, the water is filled exactly up to the spout, and a tall measuring cylinder stands under the spout to collect the overflow.
